What the official sources say

  • A taxpayer appealing a PVA real property assessment must first request a conference with the property valuation administrator or deputy, held before or during the inspection period. (KRS 133.120(1)(a) Appeal procedure; source)
  • A taxpayer still aggrieved after the PVA conference may appeal to the county board of assessment appeals by written petition to the county clerk stating reasons, identifying the property and stating the taxpayer's opinion of fair cash value. (KRS 133.120(2)(a)-(b); source)
  • The board of assessment appeals holds a public hearing for each taxpayer appeal and fixes the assessment at fair cash value. (KRS 133.120(3)(a); source)
  • A person aggrieved by the board's decision may appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals under KRS 49.220; a taxpayer who skipped the county board or failed to appear cannot appeal directly to the Board of Tax Appeals. (KRS 133.120; source)
  • Assessment standard is fair cash value; PVAs commonly use sales comparison for homes. All real property is subject to revaluation every year and each parcel must be physically inspected at least once every four years. (The Assessment Process for Real Property | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Kentucky sells certificates of delinquency (tax liens) to third-party purchasers, not the property itself; county clerks run sales from mid-July through late October. (Delinquent Property Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Counties must advertise each sale and list the certificates in the local newspaper and on the clerk's website at least 30 days before the sale. (Delinquent Property Tax | Department of Revenue; source)

Which Kentucky offices touch a property tax bill from start to finish?

Four local offices each handle one stage of the process. The property valuation administrator (PVA) puts a value on every parcel, the sheriff sends out and takes in the fall bills, the clerk's office inherits whatever stays unpaid, and the county attorney chases those leftovers.

The constitutional yardstick for the PVA is fair cash value, which the Department of Revenue describes as the price a fair voluntary sale would bring. Every parcel must be walked or physically reviewed at least once in four years, and new construction goes on the roll annually. Farm acreage can carry an agricultural value instead. Coal, oil and gas and utility property are valued by the state Office of Property Valuation rather than the PVA.

What is the way to contest a Kentucky assessment?

Begin by asking the PVA or a deputy for a conference. If that conversation leaves you unsatisfied, you file a short written petition at the clerk's office giving your reasons, the parcel you mean and the value you believe is right. Conferences can be held by telephone when you ask.

Public inspection of the roll starts the first Monday in May and lasts 13 days. Your petition must be in by the close of the next workday after the window ends. When a PVA asks and the state agrees, the cutoff can slide by up to 25 days. Bypass the local board, or miss your own hearing, and the later state appeal is off the table.

  • The local board of assessment appeals sits between 25 and 35 days after the roll closes, with a public hearing on each protest.
  • Evidence decides the outcome: sales listings, construction costs, insurance policies, mortgages or loans. A protest with no supporting facts must be denied.
  • Audio recording of the hearing is your right.
  • A paid spokesperson has to fit a role named in the statute, among them lawyer, CPA, tax consultant, licensed broker or appraiser, or be on your payroll, and needs your authorization in writing.

Filing does not pause collection. KRS 133.120(9) has you pay on the figure you claimed in the petition, and if the final value ends up higher you owe the difference plus interest. Bills are sometimes printed before an appeal wraps up, in which case your claimed value is used and a supplemental bill follows for anything the board adds.

Where does a Kentucky owner go after losing at the county board?

The next stop is the state tax appeals board, reached under KRS 49.220. A petition has to arrive inside 30 days of the mailing date on the county board's decision, and the state board rehears the matter from scratch rather than reviewing a record.

The county board owes you a written explanation whenever it changes a value, and it has to inspect the parcel in person on request from you or the PVA. The legislature amended KRS 133.120 effective July 15, 2026, so read the current wording before filing.

What does a typical Kentucky tax year look like on the calendar?

The state's standard schedule is below. Counties that mail after November 1 shift to a version with a 30 day window per stage.

Standard Kentucky real property schedule, as published by the Kentucky Department of Revenue.
DateWhat changes
Jan. 1Valuation snapshot date
Jan. 1 to Mar. 1Owners may list real property
Early May (first Monday)Roll on display for 13 days
Oct. 1 to Nov. 1Early payers save 2%
Nov. 2 to Dec. 31Face amount due
All of January5% added
Feb. 1 to Apr. 1521% added
End of day Apr. 15Unpaid bills leave the sheriff for the clerk

An owner need not re-list land and buildings each year when the prior roll already described them fully and correctly and nothing major has changed.

Who decides the rate that gets multiplied against the assessment?

Every taxing body picks its own rate, but House Bill 44 boxes in the choices. A body can roll its rate back to the compensating level, which keeps income from existing property flat, or choose a rate that lifts that income by no more than 4 percent after a public hearing. Going above the 4 percent line opens the door to a petition and a recall vote. Rates are quoted in cents for each $100 of value.

On the state side, the Department of Revenue announced a 2025 real property rate of 10.6 cents on each $100 of assessed value, down from 10.9 the year before. Assessments were projected to climb 7.54 percent, and the statute limits state revenue growth from existing property to 4 percent. Cities, school districts, counties and special districts stack their own rates on top, so the full rate varies with the parcel's location.

What are the consequences of leaving a Kentucky tax bill unpaid?

Once April 15 passes, the bill converts into a certificate of delinquency that acts as a lien. Charges then pile up by stage.

  • Interest runs 1 percent monthly.
  • A clerk fee of 10 percent and an attorney fee of 20 percent get added, though the attorney's share is forgiven when the owner pays within five business days of the clerk getting the list.
  • Notices go out from the county attorney, the first by May 15 and a second by June 15, along with payment plan offers.
  • Sales to private buyers of the certificates begin in mid-July and may run to late October, with most done by the end of August.

Using a 10 percent penalty, the sheriff's add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission, the department's worked example turns a $1,000 bill into $1,254 once it reaches the clerk. The sample total for a certificate bought by an outside investor in June reaches $1,704.21. What gets sold is the lien. The owner keeps the house but owes the buyer, who tacks on its own fees.

What property tax steps matter when a Kentucky house is being sold?

Learn the balance before the listing goes live. The sheriff can give you the amount on the current bill, and the clerk can say whether a certificate of delinquency sits against the parcel. Counties must post their delinquent lists on a county website and in the newspaper at least 30 days ahead of a sale.

The seller also owes the real estate transfer tax, a charge of $0.50 on every $500 of declared value, which the clerk takes at recording. A foreclosure transfer or a surrender in lieu of foreclosure falls outside it. A homestead exemption on the property should be reported to the PVA at transfer, and organizations with a Section 170 exemption such as churches or libraries use Revenue Form 62A023.

More questions about Kentucky Property Tax Guide

When does a Kentucky property tax bill arrive and when is it due?

Sheriffs mail bills in the fall, with collection starting October 1 or November 1 depending on the county. Payment with a 2 percent discount runs through November 1, and face value is accepted through December 31.

Until what day can I protest my valuation?

The petition is due one workday after the 13 day inspection window ends. That window starts on the first Monday in May, and a PVA conference has to happen before you file.

What penalties hit a late Kentucky bill?

January adds 5 percent, and February 1 through April 15 carries 21 percent. Afterward the bill goes to the clerk, with 1 percent monthly interest and extra fees.

Can the county sell my home over unpaid tax?

What the clerk sells is the lien, in the form of a certificate of delinquency. Your house stays yours, but you then owe the investor who bought the certificate.

Who fixes the state real property rate?

The Department of Revenue sets it each year by July 1 under KRS 132.020. For 2025 it landed at 10.6 cents on each $100 of assessed value.

Kentucky Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • To qualify, a person must be at least 65 during the tax period or classified as totally disabled; the application goes to the local PVA no later than December 31 of the eligible tax year. (DOR Sets 2025-2026 Homestead Exemption; source)
  • The applicant must own and maintain the property as a personal residence; only one exemption per residential unit is allowed. (KRS 132.810(2); source)
  • The exemption amount is adjusted every two years if the cost-of-living index has changed by at least 1%. (KRS 132.810; source)
  • When title to exempted property is transferred, the owner, executor, trustee or agent must report the transfer to the PVA; the exemption is tied to the owner, not the property, and a new owner must apply if eligible. (KRS 132.810(3)(h); The Assessment Process for Real Property; source)
  • Disabled applicants under 65 generally reapply annually, except service-connected totally disabled veterans and individuals found totally and permanently disabled under Social Security or other Kentucky statutory rules. (KRS 132.810; source)

Get My Cash Offer →

What is the Kentucky homestead exemption?

It is a deduction from the assessed value of a Kentucky home for owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Section 170 of the Kentucky Constitution created it, and the Department of Revenue says the deduction is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. Property tax is then figured on whatever value is left.

The Department gives a simple example: a house assessed at a fair cash value of $200,000 is taxed as if it were worth $150,900. The reduction applies to state, county, city and special district taxes alike. In the 2023 tax year the exemption saved more than 474,000 elderly or disabled Kentuckians about $293 million.

Who qualifies for the Kentucky homestead exemption?

Two things have to be true at once: an age or disability test, and a residence test. The statute, KRS 132.810, sets both.

  • The applicant is 65 or older during the year of the application, or was classified as totally disabled on January 1 of that year under a federal agency program or a retirement system inside or outside Kentucky.
  • The applicant owns the property and maintains it as a personal residence.
  • A disabled applicant has received disability payments and keeps the classification for the whole taxation period.
  • Only one exemption is allowed per residential unit, even when two residents both qualify.

Ownership can take several forms. Legal or equitable title, joint tenancy, tenancy in common, a condominium and certain corporate or leasehold interests of more than 98 years all count. A mobile home, an RV classified as real property or a manufactured house qualifies as a residential unit.

How and when do I apply for the exemption?

File with the property valuation administrator, the PVA, in the county where the home sits. The Department of Revenue states that applications are due by December 31 of the eligible tax year and can be submitted online, by mail or in person, depending on what the local PVA office accepts. Phone the office to learn which method it prefers.

An applicant based on age can prove it with a birth certificate, driver's license, passport or other approved document. A disability applicant needs proof of the classification. The state form is titled Application for Exemption Under the Homestead/Disability Amendment.

The valuation you write on the form cannot be used to raise your assessment. If it is, the statute requires an adjustment the next year so that your total tax comes out the same as if the increase never happened.

What if the tax bill is already paid or still unpaid when I qualify?

Timing decides whether you get a reduced bill or a refund. If you qualify before paying the bill for that year, you are entitled to a full or partial exoneration that reflects the exemption. If you qualify after paying, you are entitled to a refund of the tax on the exempt portion of the value.

This matters to heirs and to anyone selling late in the year. A seller who is eligible but never applied can ask the PVA whether an application for the current taxation period is still possible before the December 31 deadline, and can ask the sheriff how the bill would be adjusted.

How does the exemption amount change over time?

The $6,500 written into Section 170 is read as $6,500 in 1972 purchasing power. Every two years, if the federal cost of living index has moved at least 1 percent, the Department of Revenue adjusts the maximum. The 2025 and 2026 figure is $2,750 higher than the 2023 and 2024 figure.

Kentucky homestead exemption amounts. Sources: KRS 132.810 and Kentucky Department of Revenue.
PeriodMaximum exemption
Section 170 original amount (1972 dollars)$6,500
2023 and 2024 assessment years$46,350
2025 and 2026 assessment years$49,100

The department recalculates the amount every second year. Ask your PVA for the figure that applies to the tax year you are working with, since a later biennium will carry a different number.

What happens to the exemption when I sell or inherit the home?

The exemption belongs to the owner, not to the house. When title to an exempt property passes, the owner, administrator, executor, trustee, guardian, conservator or agent has to report the transfer to the PVA. A buyer or an heir who is 65 or disabled has to file a fresh application of their own.

A death also ends the period. If the person holding the classification dies before December 31, the taxation period runs only from January 1 to the date of death. A disabled owner who stops meeting the total disability classification must tell the PVA, and the exemption ends at the close of that taxation period without being prorated.

The exemption has no effect on the deed tax. The grantor still pays fifty cents per $500 of value at recording, unless the transfer falls in one of the listed exceptions such as a foreclosure or a transfer between spouses.

What should a seller with the exemption check before listing?

A few quick checks keep the paperwork clean when a house with an exemption changes hands.

  • Ask the PVA to confirm the exemption is on file for the current year and which person it is tied to.
  • Ask the sheriff for the current bill so you can see whether the exempt value was already applied.
  • Tell the PVA about the transfer once the deed is recorded, since the statute requires the owner or the estate's representative to report it.
  • If the owner has died, keep the date of death handy, because it caps the taxation period for that year.

The buyer should be told the deduction will not carry over automatically. A younger buyer will simply see a bill computed on the full assessment.

Do disabled owners under 65 have to reapply every year?

Usually yes. A totally disabled owner under 65 must apply annually. Two groups are excused after documenting the disability at the first application: service-connected totally disabled veterans of the Armed Forces, and people found totally and permanently disabled under Social Security rules, Kentucky Retirement Systems rules or another provision of the Kentucky Revised Statutes.

Missing an annual renewal can cost a year of savings, so mark December 31 on the calendar if you are in this group.

Is there a second kind of Kentucky homestead protection?

Yes, a separate one that protects against creditors. KRS 427.060 exempts an individual debtor's interest of up to $5,000 in the home the debtor or a dependent uses as a permanent residence, or in a burial plot, from sale under execution, attachment or judgment. It does not apply to foreclose a mortgage given by the owner or for purchase money, and it does not reach debts that existed before the property was bought or improved.

That $5,000 figure is far lower than the tax exemption, and the two are unrelated. The tax deduction lowers a bill; the creditor protection limits what a judgment creditor can take.

Which other property can be exempt under Section 170?

The same section lets Kentucky exempt property held by government, institutions of education, religious institutions, public libraries, cemeteries not run for private profit and institutions of purely public charity. Those owners file Revenue Form 62A023 with the PVA, who may forward unclear cases to the department. The homestead deduction for seniors and disabled owners is a different benefit with its own form.

More questions about Kentucky Homestead Exemption

How much is the Kentucky homestead exemption?

It is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. That amount comes off the assessed value of the home, and tax is figured on the rest.

What age do I have to be to claim it?

You must be 65 or older during the year you apply, or be classified as totally disabled. You also have to own the home and use it as your personal residence.

Where do I file the application?

File with the property valuation administrator in the county where the home is located. The Department of Revenue says applications are due by December 31 of the tax year.

Does the exemption transfer to the person who buys my house?

No. It follows the owner. You must report the transfer to the PVA, and a buyer or heir who is 65 or disabled needs to apply on their own.

Can I get money back if I qualified after paying my taxes?

Yes. KRS 132.810 entitles an applicant who qualifies after the bill is paid to a refund of the tax tied to the exempt value.

This guide covers what official sources say about Kentucky estate and inheritance tax.

What the official sources say

  • There is no Kentucky estate tax; Kentucky has an inheritance tax on the beneficiary's right to receive property. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Class A beneficiaries (surviving spouse, parent, child, grandchild, sibling and, under the 2026 amendment, nieces and nephews) are exempt from inheritance tax; the 2026 amendment applies to decedents dying on or after January 1, 2026. (KRS 140.070 (2026 Ky. Acts ch. 198); source)
  • Class B (e.g., daughter-in-law, son-in-law, aunt, uncle, great-grandchild) is taxed at 4% to 16%; Class C (all others) at 6% to 16%. (KRS 140.070; source)
  • Class B beneficiaries get a $1,000 exemption and Class C a $500 exemption. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • A return is due within 18 months of death; a 5% discount applies if paid within nine months, and tax over $5,000 may be paid in 10 annual installments. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • If all taxable assets pass to exempt beneficiaries and no federal Form 706 is required, an Affidavit of Exemption suffices for closing the estate. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)

Kentucky evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law.

What the official sources say

  • Under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act where adopted, for unpaid rent the landlord may terminate if rent is not paid within seven days after written notice. (KRS 383.660(2); source)
  • For other material noncompliance, the landlord may give written notice that the lease will terminate not less than 14 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied within 15 days. (KRS 383.660(1); source)
  • A landlord may not recover possession by self-help, including cutting off heat, electric, water or other essential services. (KRS 383.690; source)
  • Eviction is by forcible detainer complaint to District Court; the warrant issues to the sheriff and trial is by the court unless a party demands a jury. (KRS 383.210; source)
  • A landlord who conveys premises with a dwelling unit subject to a rental agreement in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability for events after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance. (KRS 383.600(1); source)
  • A landlord may not retake possession by self-help or by interrupting essential services. (KRS 383.690; source)
